analysis|01-01|1822|Η Α΄ Εθνοσυνέλευση της Επιδαύρου υιοθετεί το πρώτο Σύνταγμα|The First National Assembly of Epidaurus adopts the first Constitution|After the outbreak of 1821 the revolted regions were run by local administrations, such as the Peloponnesian Senate, without a common centre of power. The struggle could not be coordinated effectively, nor could it appear unified in the eyes of the European governments, which watched the revolution with reserve. The need for unified organisation and for recognition from Europe led to the convening of a national assembly at Epidaurus, where delegates from various parts of revolutionary Greece gathered. The national assembly met while the war against the Ottomans was still under way, and the need for unified administration grew ever more pressing. // The delegates voted the "Provisional Constitution of Greece", which set up legislative and executive bodies and laid down basic principles of law. At the same time national independence was proclaimed as the central aim of the struggle. The text showed the European powers of the time that the revolutionaries wanted an organised state with institutions and rules, and not a simple uprising that would end with the first military setback. The passing of the constitution did not immediately resolve the disputes, because local leaders and military commanders continued to compete for influence. // The assembly became the starting point of the country's constitutional tradition, since a series of texts that followed in the coming years began there. This constitutional effort was linked to the internal conflicts of the revolution, between politicians and military leaders, but it gave the struggle political form and cohesion. The date is according to the old calendar.

analysis|01-01|1981|Η Ελλάδα γίνεται δέκατο μέλος της Ευρωπαϊκής Οικονομικής Κοινότητας|Greece becomes the tenth member of the European Economic Community|After the Second World War Greece sought closer ties with Western Europe, and membership of the European Community became a key goal of its foreign policy. The link with the Community had already begun in the 1960s, but political instability postponed full membership. After the fall of the dictatorship in 1974 and the restoration of democracy, the government of Konstantinos Karamanlis made membership of the European Community its strategic choice. The negotiations were concluded with a treaty of accession in 1979. // With membership the country gained access to Community resources and to a large market, especially for agriculture and infrastructure, but also obligations to adapt its economy to common rules. Farmers and small businesses felt the direct effects, and the process of adjustment was not always easy. Membership was a matter of intense domestic debate, as sections of the opposition believed that the terms of accession would harm some branches of production. // The event was also regarded as a political guarantee for the stability of the young democracy, because the connection with the West limited the danger of a return to the authoritarian past. Entry into the Community shaped the country's course in the following decades and remains a point of reference for its modern European identity. Entry was linked to the active participation of the country in the common policies and decisions of the Community in the years that followed.

analysis|01-01|2001|Η Ελλάδα μπαίνει στην Ευρωζώνη|Greece joins the eurozone|During the 1990s Greece tried to reduce inflation and the deficit, so that it would meet the convergence criteria of the Maastricht Treaty. This effort was linked to the policy of the "hard drachma" and to the restriction of fiscal imbalances, which affected the daily life of many households. Monetary convergence was a necessary condition for the country to enter the common currency area. The effort had a social cost, because the fiscal adjustment affected incomes and the services of the public sector. // On 1 January 2001 the country became the twelfth member of the euro area, and the exchange rate of the drachma was locked at a fixed ratio to the new currency. Membership brought lower interest rates and easier access to borrowing, which reduced the cost of public and private loans. The rate chosen determined how competitive domestic products now were compared with partners, which affected businesses. // In the years that followed it became clear how much the economy depended on common monetary policy, since the country could no longer devalue its currency to regain competitiveness. The debt crisis after 2010 highlighted this issue in the most intense way. The debate over the role of the euro area in the Greek economy continued for decades, and so monetary membership remains a matter of political dispute.

analysis|01-01|2002|Το ευρώ μπαίνει στις τσέπες των Ελλήνων|The euro enters the pockets of the Greeks|The introduction of the euro took place in two stages: first as an accounting currency, and then with the physical circulation of banknotes and coins. Banks and services prepared for months, and citizens were informed of the conversion rates so that confusion in transactions would be avoided. The change concerned the whole of society, from the markets to wages and the tills of businesses. The conversion was complex, because cash registers, accounting systems and market price lists all had to be adjusted at the same time. // From 1 January 2002 prices and transactions were carried out in euro, and the drachma, a currency with a long history, was withdrawn after a short transitional period. Many consumers noticed price rises in daily life, and the debate about the relationship between prices and the new currency lasted for some time. During the transitional period both currencies circulated side by side, so that consumers could get used to the new prices without an abrupt change. // The change was regarded as one of the most visible steps of European integration, because the new common unit connected citizens with the European Union in their everyday lives, beyond institutional decisions. The drachma remained in the memory of many as a symbol of national monetary identity. For many citizens the euro became the first visible symbol of membership of a wider economic union, present in everyday payments.

analysis|01-01|2008|Η Κύπρος υιοθετεί το ευρώ|Cyprus adopts the euro|Cyprus had joined the European Union in 2004 and set itself the goal of a rapid entry into the euro area. To this end it had to meet the criteria for inflation, public debt and the deficit, and first to join the exchange rate mechanism. This process required steady fiscal policy and cooperation with the institutions of the Union. The Cypriot pound had for years been tied to the island's exchange rate policy, and its replacement meant the end of a national monetary responsibility. // On 1 January 2008 the euro replaced the Cypriot pound, and Malta became a member on the same day. The change strengthened Cyprus's position in Europe and facilitated trade and tourism, which were the main pillars of the island's economy. Entry into the euro area proceeded without major social unrest, because preparation had been done in good time and the banks were familiar with the conversion. // The island thus became part of the monetary policy of the euro area, with all that this meant for the possibilities of the national government. Later the economic crisis of 2013 showed how closely European support is tied to fiscal discipline. The later crisis of 2013 was connected with the island's banking sector and with the loan support that followed, which showed that monetary membership also brings constraints.

analysis|01-01|2026|Η Κύπρος αναλαμβάνει ξανά την προεδρία του Συμβουλίου της ΕΕ|Cyprus takes over the Presidency of the Council of the EU again|The Presidency of the Council of the European Union rotates every six months among the member states, in a predetermined order that ensures equality in the sequence of countries. Cyprus had held it for the first time in the second half of 2012, and its new turn coincides with the new year 2026. The post is often an opportunity for smaller states to gain more visibility in the Union's decisions. The Presidency does not concern only the country that holds it, since the decisions of the Council affect all member states and the citizens of the Union. // During the Presidency the presiding state coordinates the meetings of the Council, promotes legislation and represents the member states in negotiations with other institutions, such as the European Parliament and the Commission. This role requires diplomatic skill and a balance between different interests. Preparing the Presidency takes months of work, since priorities, the programme of meetings and meetings with partners must be set. // For a small country such as Cyprus, with the open political question of the occupation and the Cyprus problem, the post gives international visibility and an opportunity to present its priorities. Holding the Presidency can strengthen the country's credibility in Europe and bring to the fore the issues that concern it. The European dimension of the Cyprus problem remains open, and for that reason the Presidency is an opportunity to stress the country's position in favour of a solution consistent with the European acquis.

analysis|01-03|1992|Συνάντηση για το όνομα της Μακεδονίας|Meeting on the name of Macedonia|After the dissolution of Yugoslavia in 1991, the former Yugoslav republic of Macedonia became independent and wished for international recognition under the name "Macedonia". Greece reacted, fearing questions of historical identity and territorial claims, since the name of the historical region is also found on Greek soil. The dispute quickly became both an international and a domestic political issue. The name of the new state affects its language, symbols and historical memory, which is why the dispute was not limited to a diplomatic matter. // Discussions at the level of diplomats concerned the name, the symbols and the constitutional provisions of the new state, because the Greek side sought clear guarantees that there would be no irredentist references. They did not produce a solution, and the dispute remained open for almost three decades. The new state was admitted to the United Nations under a provisional name, while Greece continued to oppose the use of the name without qualification. // The interim agreement of 1995 reduced the tensions, but a final settlement came only with the Prespa Agreement in 2018. This long dispute affected relations between the two countries and the international image of the Balkan region. The long quarrel affected bilateral cooperation and remained an example of the difficulty of settling naming disputes in the Balkans.

analysis|01-03|2015|Συλλαμβάνεται ο Χριστόδουλος Ξηρός|Christodoulos Xiros is arrested|Christodoulos Xiros had been sentenced for his activity in "17 November" and had escaped from the Korydallos prison, an event that provoked reactions and debate about prison security. The escape showed that surveillance of prisoners convicted of terrorism had gaps, and the authorities had been searching for him for some time. The case was connected with the wider debate about the running of penal institutions and the management of prisoners with a history of terrorism. // The arrest took place in Monastiraki after a chase and an exchange of gunfire, and it closed a chapter that had troubled public order. The organisation "17 November" had killed dozens of people since 1975, among them politicians, judges, officers of the armed forces and diplomats. The operation in a densely populated area of central Athens increased the residents' concern about the risk of indiscriminate shooting. // The organisation had effectively been dismantled with the arrests of 2002, but the case showed that older terrorist groups still had some influence on the public debate about security. This debate returned each time a former member of the organisation left prison or escaped. Control of prisons and the handling of terrorist groups remained matters of public debate and of security legislation.

analysis|01-04|1887|Εκλογές με νικητή τον Χαρίλαο Τρικούπη|Elections won by Charilaos Trikoupis|Charilaos Trikoupis was one of the most important politicians of the 19th century, with a programme of modernising the state: railways, roads, the Corinth Canal and the strengthening of the army. His rival was Theodoros Deligiannis, and the two alternated in power in a period of intense party competition. Trikoupis linked modernisation with the country's integration into international trade, and infrastructure works were regarded as the basic tool of development. // The elections of 1887 returned him to the premiership, and his programme continued to rest on large public works. The state needed roads and lines to connect the regions and to strengthen the economy. The elections of that period reflected intense party rivalry, and the exercise of power was tied to continuous negotiations over state borrowing. // His ambitious spending, however, increased the public debt, and the country was later driven to the bankruptcy of 1893. This period is regarded as fundamental for the infrastructure of modern Greece, but also for the limits of its economic capacity, because it showed that development without matching resources is dangerous. The crisis of 1893 led to international financial supervision of public revenues, and fiscal discipline became from then on a central theme of political life.

analysis|01-04|1930|Αρχίζει η λειτουργία της Αγροτικής Τράπεζας|The Agricultural Bank begins operations|Rural Greece urgently needed cheap credit, since many farmers borrowed from usurers on harsh terms, which often led to the loss of their land. After the arrival of refugees from Asia Minor and the redistribution of land, this need became more acute, as thousands of new families needed equipment and seed. The usurers often demanded high interest rates and collateral, which drove farmers into debts from which they found it hard to escape. // The Agricultural Bank of Greece was founded in 1929 and began operating in early 1930. It gave loans for seed, tools and cultivation, and supported the transition to more organised agriculture with greater productivity. The creation of the bank was linked to the policy of settling refugees, for which agricultural credit was a necessary precondition of production. // For decades it was a basic pillar of the rural economy, and its presence in villages and towns was felt. Before being absorbed by another bank in the 2000s, it had linked its name with the development of the Greek countryside. The bank contributed to the gradual integration of rural areas into the national economy, and its work left its mark on village life.

analysis|01-04|1956|Ο Καραμανλής ιδρύει την Εθνική Ριζοσπαστική Ένωση|Karamanlis founds the National Radical Union|After the death of Alexandros Papagos in 1955, King Paul appointed Konstantinos Karamanlis as prime minister rather than the old politicians, who had a long presence in power. The new prime minister needed his own party organisation to support his political work and not depend on the old party forces. Karamanlis was already known as a politician who had taken part in the governments of the 1950s, so his mandate was clear. // Thus the National Radical Union was founded, which won the elections of 1956 and governed until 1963. During its rule infrastructure works and efforts at economic development took place, while the country was strengthened in its ties with the West, at a time when European integration was beginning to take shape. The government was linked to the creation of new roads and the improvement of transport, but also to political polarisation between pro-government and opposition forces. // The party was also linked with periods of intense political tension and with accusations of electoral fraud in 1961. That experience showed how critical trust in electoral procedures was for the legitimacy of power. The success of ERE in the elections of 1956 showed how strong Karamanlis's political leadership was, but also how difficult it was to maintain trust in an electoral climate of tension.

analysis|01-05|1913|Η ναυμαχία της Λήμνου|The naval battle of Lemnos|During the First Balkan War the Greek fleet had blockaded the Dardanelles, in order to limit the ability of the Ottoman army to be reinforced from the sea. The Ottoman fleet tried to break the blockade, so as to regain control of the Aegean and protect its sea transport. The blockade of the Dardanelles was part of the wider strategy of the Greek fleet, which aimed to cut off the supply of the Ottoman Empire in the Aegean. // In the naval battle of Lemnos Pavlos Kountouriotis, with the battleship "Averof" leading, forced the Turkish ships to withdraw, with losses for the Ottomans. The naval superiority of the Greek fleet was decisive for completing the campaign in the Aegean. This naval operation was linked to the developments of the First Balkan War, in which coordination at sea and on land was a critical factor. // The victory secured Greece control of the sea and allowed the liberation of Aegean islands, which were added to the Greek state. It also showed the importance of investing in a modern navy, which had acquired great significance for the country's defence. The experience of the naval battle influenced later decisions on naval armament, and the role of the sea for the country became clearer from then on.

analysis|01-06|1821|Ο Κολοκοτρώνης στη Μάνη|Kolokotronis in Mani|Theodoros Kolokotronis had served in the Ionian Islands in the British army and was already known as a warrior with experience of battles. The Philiki Etaireia was preparing the Revolution, and the role of the Peloponnesian chieftains was critical to the success of the plan. The Philiki Etaireia, founded in Odessa in 1814, gathered members from various social strata and prepared the uprising in many parts of Greece. // On his return to Mani Kolokotronis gave impetus to the organisation of the uprising, while the local notables and captains prepared for the clash. The organisation rested on networks of local trust, which he knew well. The chieftains of the Peloponnese had their own networks of influence, and their cooperation with the notables was necessary for organising the forces in the field. // Mani and Messenia formed the first core of the Revolution in the Peloponnese in March. His presence made it clear that the uprising would not depend only on the notables, but also on the military men, who would determine operations in the field. Kolokotronis later became one of the most important military figures of the Revolution, and his image remains linked with the struggle of the first period.

analysis|01-06|1948|Τελειώνει η μάχη της Κόνιτσας|The battle of Konitsa ends|During the Civil War the Democratic Army wanted a town that would serve as the seat of its provisional government, so as to gain political legitimacy within the country. Konitsa, close to the Albanian border, was an attractive target for reasons of geography and supply. The area was mountainous and isolated, so holding the town required continuous supply and secure lines of communication. // The attack took place at the end of 1947 and in early 1948. The National Army held out with reinforcements and with the help of the air force, which played an important role in stopping attacks in the mountains. The mountain passes restricted the movements of infantry, and the role of air support in operations in the mountains grew. // The guerrillas were forced to withdraw with heavy losses. The failure deprived the Democratic Army of the possibility of controlling a town, and showed the limits of its strength against an organised army with air support. This battle is important for the study of the Civil War, because it shows that the outcome did not depend only on guerrilla action but also on control of the ground. The operation was one of the last major episodes of the conflict in northern Greece.

analysis|01-08|1991|Δολοφονείται ο εκπαιδευτικός Νίκος Τεμπονέρας|The teacher Nikos Temponeras is murdered|At the end of 1990 pupils occupied schools across the country, protesting against the new system of university entrance and against the conditions in schools. The New Democracy government was in conflict with the movement, and the issue dominated public debate. The student movement had both a trade-union and a political dimension, and the confrontation with the government played out in public discourse throughout its course. // Nikos Temponeras, a teacher, was attacked in Patras by people linked with the right and died, an event that caused great outrage. The victim immediately became a symbol of the violence that accompanied political confrontation in that period. The murder provoked protests in many cities, and the government found itself in a difficult position on the question of political responsibility for the violence. // The event caused mass demonstrations, and his name became a symbol for the student and pupil movement. Each year his memory is honoured by pupils and teachers, and it reminds people of the limits of political violence in democratic life. His memory is today invoked in the debate on the safety of teachers and on the importance of peaceful political participation by young people.

analysis|01-09|475|Ο Ζήνων φεύγει από την Κωνσταντινούπολη|Zeno flees Constantinople|Zeno, of Isaurian origin, had become emperor of the Eastern Roman state with the support of the army, but he was disliked in Constantinople because he was a foreigner in the eyes of the capital. His power rested mainly on the military, while the court and the city viewed him with suspicion. Zeno's rise rested on the Isaurian military corps and on allies in the court, while the absence of a broad social base made him vulnerable. // Relatives of the former emperor Leo I conspired against him, and Basiliscus, brother of Leo's widow, was proclaimed emperor. Zeno was forced to leave, while the succession became the object of disputes between the elite families. Basiliscus had the support of the empress Verina, widow of Leo, and the temporary overthrow of Zeno showed how fragile the balance in Constantinople was. // Zeno managed to regain the throne shortly afterwards, in 476. The events show the instability that characterised the era and the role of military and dynastic factions in the succession, as well as how easily a power could be overthrown. Zeno's return in 476 showed that the support of the army could prevail over dynastic claims, even if only temporarily.

analysis|01-09|1938|Γάμος του διαδόχου Παύλου με τη Φρειδερίκη|Wedding of Crown Prince Paul to Frederica|After the restoration of the monarchy in 1935, the royal family wanted to secure the succession in a politically unstable environment. Crown Prince Paul, brother of King George II, married Princess Frederica of Hanover, a young woman who belonged to a German princely house. The marriage also had diplomatic significance for the monarchy's ties. The wedding followed the period of political uncertainty of the interwar years, and the succession was a critical question for the stability of the institution. // The couple had children, among them the future King Constantine II. Paul became king in 1947, at a time when the country was at the end of the Civil War and in the midst of reconstruction. Frederica was a member of European nobility, and her presence in Greece was linked with the international relations of the royal family. // Frederica had a strong presence in public life, with charitable initiatives that reached many people, but also with reactions to her political influence. Her figure remains a subject of discussion about the role of the royal family in post-war Greece. The royal family was at the centre of disputes over the institution of the monarchy, which was finally abolished in the 1970s.

analysis|01-09|1965|Επίσημα στοιχεία για τους Έλληνες της Κωνσταντινούπολης|Official figures on the Greeks of Constantinople|Relations between Greece and Turkey deteriorated in the 1960s because of the Cyprus question, and this tension directly affected the Greek communities of Constantinople. In 1964 Turkey denounced the settlement treaty of 1930 and expelled Greek nationals from Constantinople, as part of wider pressure on Athens. The treaty of 1930 had regulated the settlement rights of residents and was regarded as an important step in Greek-Turkish relations of the interwar period. // The figures announced in Athens showed the size of the problem: thousands of people lost their homes, their businesses and their property and left the city where they lived. Most could not take their belongings with them. Those expelled often could not transfer their property, and compensation was difficult or impossible, which burdened their financial situation. // The expulsion led to a further decline of the Greek community, which had already been hit by the events of 1955. This development radically changed the composition of the city, and its memory remains alive among refugee families. The Greek community of the City, with a presence of centuries, now numbered fewer people, and its cultural presence in the city was considerably reduced.

analysis|01-10|1941|Ο ελληνικός στρατός καταλαμβάνει την Κλεισούρα|The Greek army takes Klisoura|After the Italian invasion from Albania in October 1940, the Greek army repelled the invaders and entered Albanian territory, in a campaign that caused widespread optimism in Greece. The winter and the mountainous terrain hindered operations, and the army faced a shortage of supplies. The Italian attack had caught the country by surprise, but the Greek army mobilised quickly, and the successful resistance provoked wide national emotion. // Klisoura was a strategic point, since the crossing towards Vlore was controlled from there. Its capture was an important success, but it did not lead to final victory, since conditions and the lack of supplies restricted the advance. The snowbound passes and mountainous Epirus burdened transport, because ammunition and food did not reach the units at the front easily. // In April the German invasion changed the situation at the front, since the Greek army had to face two opponents at different points at the same time. This change led to a rapid reversal of the situation. The German attack from Bulgaria placed the Greek army at risk of encirclement, and withdrawal from Albanian territory became necessary.

analysis|01-12|1957|Πρεμιέρα της ταινίας «Το κορίτσι με τα παραμύθια»|Premiere of the film "The Girl with the Fairy Tales"|The 1950s were a period of growth for Greek cinema, with many productions each year and an enthusiastic audience in the cinemas. Films of that time often combined social drama, comedy and song, and were addressed to a broad audience looking for entertainment after the difficult decades of war. Greek cinema of the period rested on commercial productions aimed at a wide public, and collaboration between actors, directors and screenwriters was frequent. // The premiere of "The Girl with the Fairy Tales" fits into this climate, when the cinemas of Athens were full and actors became stars of popular entertainment. The production of such works contributed to the creation of a shared cultural experience. Viewers went to the cinema as a social experience, and films were discussed among friends and in the neighbourhood. // This genre later gave an image of Greek post-war society, and it remains beloved on television and in the memories of the audience. Films of the period are today a source for the study of the customs, language and values of that era. Films of the period are now a subject of study for the history of society, and many of them are shown again on television.

analysis|01-13|532|Η στάση του Νίκα|The Nika riot|The empire of Justinian was in a phase of ambitious plans, with wars and costly works that required large resources. The taxes needed for these, and the power of high officials, provoked anger among the population of the capital, which was ready to express its discontent. Justinian sought to restore the empire through campaigns and legislative work, and the costs of these plans were enormous for the state. // The uprising peaked in the Hippodrome, where the generals Belisarius and Mundus attacked the crowd and killed a large number of people. Before this, the empress Theodora is said to have persuaded her husband to stay, and the emperor's position remained secure. The revolt left destruction in a large part of the capital, and reconstruction was carried out through large public works. // After the revolt Justinian rebuilt from the beginning Hagia Sophia, which had burned during the disturbances, and this work became a symbol of imperial power. His authority became more unassailable, and the building became a monument of Byzantine architecture. The dome of Hagia Sophia was a technical achievement of its age, and the monument remains one of the most important in Constantinople.

analysis|01-13|1962|Ο Ιάκωβος εκλέγεται αρχιεπίσκοπος Αθηνών|Iakovos is elected Archbishop of Athens|The Church of Greece elects its archbishop through the Hierarchy, that is, the whole body of senior clergy, and the elections were often linked with political and ecclesiastical disputes. The period was turbulent for the institution, which operated within the framework of the autocephalous Greek Church. The Hierarchy of the Church of Greece meets with the participation of the metropolitans, and the election of the archbishop is its basic responsibility. // Iakovos's election was not calm, since accusations against him soon emerged and the matter reached the ecclesiastical court. This development provoked debate both inside and outside the clergy. In such cases the credibility of the institutions is often judged, since public opinion expects transparency and cohesion from the leadership of the Church. // The incident shows that relations between Church and state in post-war Greece were not always stable, and that personal issues could affect the leadership of the institution. The affair showed how carefully ecclesiastical procedures must operate in order to keep the trust of the faithful. Today the Constitution recognises the Orthodox Christian Church as the prevailing religion, and relations with the state are regulated on the basis of this framework.

analysis|01-13|1968|Σφοδρό ψύχος και ναυάγια στην Ελλάδα|Severe cold and shipwrecks in Greece|The winter of 1968 was particularly harsh in Greece, with snowfall and low temperatures that affected the whole country. Macedonia and Thrace were hit most strongly, and the road network and infrastructure of the time were vulnerable to the weather. The snowfalls affected crops and livestock farming in the mountain areas, and farmers suffered damage to their animals and storehouses. // The declaration of a state of emergency helped mobilise the state to assist those affected, but many communities suffered for days, with villages cut off and power cuts. The road-clearing services and the maintenance of power lines were severely tested, and restoring the damage took considerable time. Extreme temperatures also affected the health of the elderly, since heating and the transport of firewood were difficult in many mountain villages. // At the same time the bad weather caused shipwrecks, such as that of the freighter "Evelpis" at Navarino. Phenomena of this kind reminded people how important preparation is against extreme weather events, especially in a country with many islands and mountain areas. The emergency shows the importance of forecasting systems and civil protection, so that citizens are informed of risks in good time.

analysis|01-13|1997|Ανακαλύπτεται το Λύκειο του Αριστοτέλη|The Lyceum of Aristotle is discovered|The Lyceum was a school of philosophy founded by Aristotle in Athens, near the sanctuary of Apollo Lykeios, after 335 BC. There the philosopher taught and gathered pupils, and the school became one of the most important centres of ancient science and philosophy. The school had a stoa and a peripatos, from which the name of the Peripatetic philosophers derived. // Its exact location had been unknown for centuries, despite the sources that mention it, and many scholars tried to locate it without success. This ignorance made the subject all the more interesting for archaeology. Excavations helped to compare the written sources with the finds, and archaeologists were able to interpret the use of the buildings better. // The discovery was made during the construction of the Museum of Contemporary Art, when archaeologists found the ruins of a palaestra and other buildings. The find gave substantial information about the layout of the spaces where philosophy and natural science were taught, and today the archaeological site is open to visitors. The site has been integrated into the modern city, and its presence recalls the continuity of the Greek philosophical tradition up to our own time.

analysis|01-14|1822|Ο Κολοκοτρώνης καταλαμβάνει τον Ακροκόρινθο|Kolokotronis captures Acrocorinth|Acrocorinth was a strong fortress that controlled access to the Peloponnese from the Isthmus, and for that reason it was a critical point for any army. It remained in Ottoman hands in 1821 and was a strategic target for the revolutionaries, who wished to control the passage to the southern peninsula. The fortress stands on a height above ancient Corinth and allowed control of the roads that linked the mainland with southern Greece. The position of the fortress, on a steep rock above Corinth, made its capture difficult with the means of the age. // After a siege and uncertain negotiations, the castle passed to the Greeks, who thus secured an important position in the struggle. The capture helped to control the Isthmus, with obvious advantages for the coordination of forces. The need to control the Isthmus was a constant one, since military and commercial movements from mainland Greece to the Peloponnese passed through it. // Although in 1822 the forces of Dramali invaded the Peloponnese, the fortress remained in Greek hands. It became a symbol of Greek resilience and a monument that visitors still see today. The history of the fortress, with its successive dominations by the Byzantine, Venetian and Ottoman periods, is a point of reference for the historical memory of the area.

analysis|01-14|1943|Σκοτώνεται ο Ιωάννης Τσιγάντες|Ioannis Tsigantes is killed|During the Occupation many intelligence organisations that cooperated with the Allies were developed in Greece, and the network "Midas 614" was among the best known. It supplied information about Axis movements, which helped Allied operations in the Mediterranean, in a period when information was of decisive importance. These networks often operated from the Middle East, with radio communications and hidden refuges, so that information could be passed on to the Allies. // Ioannis Tsigantes, a naval officer, was the leader of the network and organised the collection and transmission of data. His activity required great caution, since any mistake could lead to arrest. Cooperation with the Allied services was critical, because the evaluation of the data and the rescue of the network's people required coordination. The success of the networks depended on the security of contacts and on the steady cooperation of their members. // He was killed in Athens after being betrayed, and many members of the organisation were arrested. His sacrifice is characteristic of the role of the secret resistance, which worked without publicity and at great personal risk. The memory of the members of the secret resistance is honoured today in events and monuments, and historical research highlights its importance for the end of the war.

analysis|01-15|1822|Ο Δημήτριος Υψηλάντης εκλέγεται πρόεδρος του Βουλευτικού|Dimitrios Ypsilantis is elected president of the Vouleutiko|The First National Assembly of Epidaurus created two organs of power: the Executive, with Alexandros Mavrokordatos as president, and the Vouleutiko, which carried out legislative work.
